issue: Whether pumped storage plants (PSPs) should be added to the categories of generating stations eligible to participate in the High Price Day Ahead Market (HP-DAM) on the power exchanges.
outcome: The Commission formed a prima facie view in favour and proposed including PSPs as an eligible HP-DAM category. It initiated suo motu proceedings under Regulation 56 of the Conduct of Business Regulations, 2023, issued a public notice, and directed parties to file written submissions within 15 days. No final decision has been taken.
summary: CERC has proposed that pumped storage plants (PSPs) be allowed to sell in the High Price Day Ahead Market (HP-DAM), which is currently open only to gas stations using imported RLNG or naphtha, imported-coal stations and battery storage. The proposal follows NLDC recommendations of July 2026 and a Ministry of Power letter of 30.07.2026. NLDC's analysis noted that operational PSP capacity (7,425.6 MW) is largely tied up, and that HP-DAM cleared on only 47 days between April 2025 and July 2026. It also found a solar-hour to evening-peak price spread in the DAM of about ₹4.37 per unit. The Commission took the prima facie view that the DAM alone may not give PSPs enough opportunity and that HP-DAM access could improve their viability and support grid flexibility. This is a proposal, not a final order: CERC has started suo motu proceedings, issued a public notice, and asked parties to file written submissions within 15 days of the order dated 28.10.2026.
headline: CERC proposes letting pumped storage plants sell in the high-price day-ahead market

issue: Whether to defer again the start of Regulation 9(7)(ii) of the DSM Regulations, 2024, under which a deficit in the Deviation and Ancillary Service (DAS) Pool Account is recovered from drawee DICs in the ratio of the shortfall of reserves allocated by NLDC.
outcome: Using its power to remove difficulty under Regulation 12, the Commission kept the existing recovery basis in Regulation 9(7)(i) in force until 04.04.2027 and deferred Regulation 9(7)(ii) to 05.04.2027. Grid-India must submit the detailed recovery procedure for approval before 04.04.2027.

summary: CERC has deferred, for a second time, the change in how deficits in the Deviation and Ancillary Service (DAS) Pool Account are recovered from drawee DICs. Under Regulation 9(7) of the DSM Regulations, 2024, a deficit not covered by other regions' pool surpluses is recovered 50% by drawal at the ISTS periphery and 50% by GNA; from the second stage, it was to be recovered in proportion to each DIC's shortfall of reserves allocated by NLDC. The second stage had already been moved to 05.10.2026 by the order in Petition No. 02/SM/2026. Grid-India reported on 29.09.2026 that state-level reserve frameworks are not ready and that only 7 of 34 States/entities had furnished reserve information. Acting suo motu under Regulation 12 (power to remove difficulty), the Commission kept the first-stage basis in force until 04.04.2027 and deferred the reserve-shortfall basis to 05.04.2027. Grid-India must prepare the detailed recovery procedure and methodology before 04.04.2027 for the Commission's approval.

summary: CERC has adopted the tariffs discovered in SJVN's tender for firm and dispatchable round-the-clock (FDRE) power from ISTS-connected renewable projects, under the Ministry of Power's FDRE guidelines of 09.06.2023. Although 1,200 MW was tendered, five bidders offered only 560 MW, and under the tender rules 448 MW was awarded. The tariffs are ReNew Solar Power ₹4.82 for 100 MW, EG Energy Development ₹4.83 for 60 MW and Dineshchandra R Agrawal Infracon ₹4.86 for 100 MW. summary: CERC has extended the scheduled commercial operation date of Mounting Renewable Power's 250 MW wind-solar hybrid project at Jamnagar, Gujarat, from 30.06.2025 to 30.06.2026. The project supplies power to Welspun Living and Welspun Corp under PPAs dated 26.02.2024. The petitioners cited delays in transmission bays, right-of-way disputes on the dedicated line, land allotment, and the effects of cyclone Biparjoy and heavy rainfall. Because the PPAs were not under Section 63 bidding, the extension fell to the Commission on the recommendation of the Committee it set up under Regulation 13(2)(h) of the 2020 Sharing Regulations. The Committee's report of 19.06.2026 found the delay not attributable to the generator. The Commission adopted that recommendation and allowed the waiver of inter-State transmission charges as if COD had been 30.06.2025. The waiver covers only the capacity that achieved COD by 30.06.2026: the petitioner reported 174.9 MW of the planned 250 MW. NLDC must verify the COD certificates before allowing the waiver.

summary: CERC has rejected Vena Energy's plea to treat its 160 MW blended wind project in Koppal, Karnataka (129.6 MW wind, 30.4 MW solar) as a wind generator for deviation settlement. The project was bid under MNRE's 2020 Blended Wind Guidelines and commissioned on 29.10.2024. SRPC treats it as a hybrid because it has wind and solar behind one injection point, which puts it in the tighter deviation band for solar and hybrid sellers under Regulation 8(4) of the DSM Regulations, 2024. Vena said this raised its DSM liability to about 5.3% of revenue, against about 3.0% if treated as wind. The Commission held that qualifying under the Blended Wind Guidelines does not decide treatment under the DSM Regulations. The 33% hybrid threshold in other guidelines is not relevant either, and the developer could have built a wind-only project, as another bidder in the same tranche did. Crucially, the Commission said its powers to relax and remove difficulty under Regulations 11 and 12 cannot be used to create a new category of generating station.
headline: Vena's blended wind project stays in the tighter hybrid deviation band

summary: UPERC has approved Noida Power Company's plan to buy 300 MW of firm and dispatchable renewable power round the clock for 25 years, with supply from December 2028, under the Ministry of Power's FDRE Guidelines. The Commission linked the purchase to the long-term firm capacity it had directed NPCL to secure in June 2026. It accepted NPCL's deviation to award the entire 300 MW to one bidder, reasoning that splitting a small quantum would lose economies of scale. That is allowed only at the L1 tariff; otherwise capacity goes to bidders within L1 plus 2%. Bidding is restricted to developers holding a final connectivity grant from the CTU or STU with a start date on or before 31.12.2028. Storage may be tied up with a third party, though the developer stays fully liable under the PPA. Consortium finances are assessed in aggregate, and a debarment clause mirroring Rule 8 of the Late Payment Surcharge Rules, 2022 was found consistent. NPCL must align its PPA's due date, rebate and dispute clauses with SECI's documents.

summary: GERC has refused interim protection to Stockwell Energy Vault Four, which won a 65 MW/130 MWh standalone battery project at GUVNL's Vasedi substation under the Phase VII tender and missed the 17 September 2026 financial closure date. The developer had claimed force majeure from the West Asia war, relying on a Ministry of Finance office memorandum of 29 April 2026 and Ministry of Power advisories. On the bank guarantee of Rs 8,12,50,000, the Commission applied the settled test: an unconditional guarantee is stopped only for egregious fraud or special equities, and loss of the project and its viability gap funding is a commercial consequence, not irreparable harm. It also declined a free stay on termination, noting GUVNL's objection that other developers in the same tender reached financial closure and that the developer had not shown how the war prevented financial closure as distinct from commissioning. Instead it let the developer use the contract's own extension route: apply within 15 days and pay Rs 1,000 per MW per day in advance for the whole extension. Payment is without prejudice to the force majeure claim, which the main petition will decide.
headline: GERC will not stop GUVNL encashing a BESS developer's guarantee over force majeure

summary: RERC has dismissed Shree Cement's petition under Section 142 against JVVNL. Shree Cement's Jobner grinding unit has a contract demand of 7.40 MVA and a 7.08 MW behind-the-meter captive solar plant commissioned in March 2023. It asked JVVNL to reduce its contract demand to 3,540 kVA and add BESS, relying on the fourth and fifth provisos to Regulation 5(ii) of the RERC (Terms and Conditions for Green Energy Open Access) Regulations, 2025, which allow captive RE capacity up to 200% of contract demand with BESS for energy from capacity above 100%. JVVNL refused. The Commission held that the GEOA Regulations deal expressly with existing plants through the one-time conversion option in Regulation 7, so the saving clause in Regulation 31 cannot be used to bring in the 200% limit for a plant that stays under the earlier regime, where captive capacity was capped at 100% of contract demand. Read with its object, the enhanced limit is meant to encourage additional RE capacity, not to let a consumer reduce contract demand and fixed charges with no new capacity. RERC agreed that, on a plain reading, the provisos limit a behind-the-meter plant to contract demand, and noted that the petitioner had made the same suggestion in the GEOA procedure hearings (order of 12.12.2025) without disclosing it.
headline: RERC refuses Shree Cement's bid to cut contract demand under the 200% captive limit

summary: RERC has approved RUVITL's purchase, for the Rajasthan Discoms, of up to 1,300 MW from the Government of Himachal Pradesh through PTC India for November 2026 to February 2027. The power is hydro, scheduled day-ahead and concentrated in morning and evening peaks, at Rs 15.50/kWh including trading margin at the seller's CTU periphery; with ISTS charges and losses the landed cost is about Rs 16.62/kWh. RUVITL cited a supply crisis from September 2026: average demand of about 14,518 MW against 12,340 MW a year earlier, peak demand of 17,557 MW, RVUNL availability well below plan, coal constraints, and exchange and DEEP portal tenders that drew no or limited response or higher effective peak prices. SLDC supported the petition on grid security grounds, citing NRLDC alerts for overdrawal. title: Captive Power Producers Association

parties.name: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE)

issue: Whether CERC should revise its 18 February 2020 methodology for estimating electricity generated from biomass in coal plants that co-fire biomass, so that captive co-generation plants, which use part of their heat for steam, get more renewable purchase obligation credit.
outcome: Rejected. The Commission had already considered and decided the co-generation point in 2020, and CPPA placed only one month's data from one member's plant on record, which does not show the methodology is unsuitable.
summary: CERC has refused to change how biomass co-firing is credited in captive co-generation plants. The Captive Power Producers Association, representing industries in Maharashtra and Gujarat, argued that the 2020 methodology, which counts biomass electricity in proportion to biomass heat input, gives co-generation plants less RPO credit than conventional plants for the same biomass, because part of their heat goes to process steam. It proposed basing the credit on fuel used for power only, using steam enthalpy or a normative heat rate. The Commission found that CPPA had made the same proposal in 2020 and that the order then applied the heat-input principle to co-generation plants on purpose. CPPA said three years of data showed the problem but filed only one month's data from one member's plant. The Commission said it can revisit a methodology when the record warrants it, but found no basis here. MNRE did not appear.
headline: CERC keeps its biomass co-firing credit method for captive co-generation plants

outcome: Rejected. An extension under Regulation 13(2)(h) can run at most to 30 June 2026 and helps only if the project reaches COD by the extended date. None of the four projects did, and all expect COD after 30 June 2026, so they get only the graded waiver under Regulation 13(2)(a) once commissioned.

All had a scheduled COD of 1 June 2025 and were held up because the common transmission system needed for their GNA was late; CTUIL put the anticipated dates between 30 June 2026 and 30 April 2027. The Commission's committee had recommended extending the scheduled COD to 31 May 2026 or until the system was ready. CERC held that Regulation 13(2)(h) allows at most two six-month extensions beyond 30 June 2025, so the latest possible date is 30 June 2026, and the extended waiver applies only if COD is achieved by then. Since every project expects COD after that date, none qualifies; each will get the graded waiver under Regulation 13(2)(a) when it is commissioned.

title: Tata Power Renewable Energy Limited

parties.name: Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)

issue: Whether Tata Power Renewable's 198 MW wind project at Karur, Tamil Nadu, with a scheduled COD of 1 June 2025 and delayed by the common transmission system, should have its scheduled COD treated as 4 February 2026 so that it keeps the full ISTS charge waiver.
outcome: Allowed. The committee had extended the scheduled COD to 4 February 2026 and the project reached full COD that day, so all three conditions of Regulation 13(2)(h) are met and the project gets the waiver as if it had reached COD by 30 June 2025.
summary: CERC has confirmed the full ISTS charge waiver for Tata Power Renewable's 198 MW wind project at Karur, Tamil Nadu, built for captive supply to Tata Steel. The project's scheduled COD was 1 June 2025; it was commissioned in stages from 16 October 2025, with the last 10.8 MW on 2 February 2026, while the common transmission system and right-of-way disputes held up evacuation. The Commission's committee recommended treating the scheduled COD as 4 February 2026. The Commission set out the three conditions of Regulation 13(2)(h): a scheduled COD on or before 30 June 2025, a delay from force majeure or reasons not attributable to the generator, and COD on or before the extended date, with no more than two six-month extensions. All three were met, so the project is treated as if it had reached COD by 30 June 2025.
headline: Tata Power's 198 MW Karur wind project keeps the full ISTS waiver

summary: CERC has revived the Rajasthan Solarpark Development Company's application to add 925 MW of battery storage to the 925 MW Nokh solar park at Bhadla-II, using the existing connectivity for non-solar hours under the right of first refusal introduced by the third amendment to the GNA Regulations.
